title: Slice isolation latency profiling — experimental notes
body:
Purpose and scope:
This note captures an experimental run investigating slice-level isolation strategies in the continuous batching scheduler. The focus was to profile hotspots, measure tail-latency behavior under mixed workloads, and evaluate isolation knobs that aim to reduce cross-traffic amplification during microbursts. This is a working artefact — results below are preliminary and meant to guide follow-up experiments.

Background / motivation:
We've observed recurring 95th-99.9th percentile spikes when medium-priority long-sequence requests coincide with short interactive queries. Continuous batching is efficient for throughput but can amplify queueing delays when a few long requests occupy batch capacity. Prior experiments focused on windowing and timeouts; here we explore an orthogonal idea: "slice isolation" — treat a single batch as logically partitioned slices that can be reserved or steered to reduce interference.

Hypotheses:
- H1: Enforcing per-slice admission caps (max tokens or max requests per slice) will reduce 99.9th latency for short queries without raising median latency significantly.
- H2: A lightweight preemption policy for pending long-request KV cache fills can reduce tail latency more than strict timeouts.
- H3: Slice-aware fairness that weights slices by recent latency violations reduces oscillation compared to simple round-robin slice rotation.

Experiment matrix summary:
- Workloads: mixed (70% short chat requests, 30% long generation, sequence lengths sampled: short 8–64 tokens, long 1024–2048 tokens).
- QPS envelope: steady 500 qps with periodic microbursts to 1800 qps (10s spurts every 5m).
- Hardware: 8xA100 pool, same model (gptx-7b-quant) across nodes.
- Runtime build: serving-runtime@2025-09-10+slice-proto (PR 456).
- Metrics captured: p50/p90/p95/p99/p99.9 latency, batch occupancy, batch formation time, tokens/sec, scheduler loop CPU, kernel-level time breakdown (flamegraphs), KV cache hit rate, memory pressure events.

Scheduler variants tested (labels):
- base-continuous: current production continuous-batching config (baseline).
- slice-cap-4: batches sliced into 4 logical slots, admission cap 2 requests / slice, token-cap 256 tokens/slice.
- slice-cap-8: 8 slices, admission cap 1 request / slice, token-cap 512 tokens/slice (higher token cap per slice to let long ones still use capacity).
- slice-preempt: like slice-cap-4 but allows preempt of longest pending request in the slice if a short request has waited > 15ms (preempt penalty 5ms).
- slice-fairness-adapt: slice-cap-4 plus adaptive weights: slices that see p99 > target backoff get 20% more admission the following 30s.

Key tunables (examples used in runs):
- batch_timeout_ms: 12 (baseline), 8 (aggressive), 20 (lenient) — we used 12 for most runs.
- slice_count: 4 | 8
- slice_request_cap: 1 | 2
- slice_token_cap: 256 | 512
- preempt_threshold_ms: 15
- fairness_window_s: 30

Representative profiling notes (flamegraph highlights):
- Kernel time distribution: attention kernels dominated token compute as expected (~68% of kernel time).
- Scheduler overhead: continuous loop accounted for ~1.6% CPU per GPU-stream; slice bookkeeping added ~0.9% (slice-cap-8 peak).
- KV cache insertion: long-request cache fills introduced spikes in host-to-device memcpy contention during batch assembly windows. These align tightly with tail spikes.
- Preemption bookkeeping added lock contention on the pending-queue lock in naive implementation — we observed a 12% increase in scheduler lock wait time in slice-preempt runs.

Results summary (p99/p99.9 focus):
- base-continuous: p99 = 145ms, p99.9 = 720ms (during microbursts p99.9 up to 1.3s). Median 18ms.
- slice-cap-4: p99 = 120ms, p99.9 = 420ms. Median 20ms (+2ms overhead). Batch occupancy slightly reduced (~8% lower tokens/batch).
- slice-cap-8: p99 = 110ms, p99.9 = 390ms. Median 22ms. Overhead slightly higher due to extra slice management.
- slice-preempt: p99 = 102ms, p99.9 = 260ms. Notable improvement in p99.9 but added scheduler CPU and lock contention.
- slice-fairness-adapt: p99 = 108ms, p99.9 = 300ms. Reduced oscillation compared to slice-preempt (less variance in p95->p99 transitions).

Operational observations:
- Tradeoff: isolation reduced high-percentile latency at the cost of small median regressions and lower effective throughput in short windows. For PLG customers this tradeoff seems acceptable when they prioritize interactivity.
- Preemption is effective but requires lock-free or less-contended data structures; current naive implementation increases scheduler jitter.
- KV cache fill behavior is critical: heavy cache inserts from long requests correlate with memcpy stalls that affect all slices; offloading cache writes to a background thread pool mitigates a large portion of the tail spikes.

Follow-up micro-experiments planned:
- Implement lock-free pending-queue (Michael-Scott queue) for preemptible path and re-run slice-preempt to validate lock contention reduction.
- Background KV cache writer: move cache inserts off the critical batch assembly path, measure p99.9 delta.
- Dynamic slice sizing: allow slice_token_cap to stretch when system utilization < 70%, shrink otherwise. Rapid elasticity could preserve throughput while protecting short queries.
- Compare with aggressive batch_timeout_ms=8 + slice-cap-4 to see if combined short timeouts + slice isolation is strictly better than either alone.

Immediate actionable recommendations (short list):
1) Ship slice-cap-4 as an opt-in scheduler policy behind a feature flag for a subset of Hosted API customers who request improved interactivity (internal rollout to beta).
2) Prioritize implementing lock-free pending-queue before enabling preemption broadly.
3) Prototype background KV cache writer in the serving-runtime repo and run a focused benchmark with synthetic long-request patterns.
4) Add metric: per-slice pending-queue-age histogram to identify when slices are starved.

Open questions / unknowns:
- How do these slice policies interact with model-quantization-related variability (int8 paths may shift compute vs memcpy balance)?
- What are the UX knobs for customers to tune slice behavior? (expose simple "interactive" vs "throughput" profiles?)
- Cost impact: isolation lowers tokens/sec in microburst windows; need to estimate billing effects and potential compensating autoscaling behavior for Dedicated customers.

Raw experiment log excerpt (timestamps are wall-clock during run):
[2025-09-22T14:03:12Z] start run slice-cap-4, microburst schedule active
[2025-09-22T14:03:35Z] microburst spike -> qps 1792, p99.9 observed 0.47s
[2025-09-22T14:04:02Z] batch_assemble: observed memcpy_stall=18ms, affected_batches=22
[2025-09-22T14:06:10Z] slice-preempt demo: preempted 34 long requests, observed scheduler_lock_wait +12%

Notes to self / next steps for the doc owner:
- Pair with SRE to run long-duration soak (24h) with slice-cap-4 on a trimmed customer-shaped trace.
- Add a short Jupyter notebook that plots per-slice latency distributions (p50/p90/p99) and include in Confluence page (CONFLUENCE-RT-1423).
- Draft beta rollout announcement with fallback toggle and observability playbook.

References and links:
- Design sketch: CONFLUENCE-RT-1423 (slice isolation design)
- PR with prototype: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/456
- Related tickets: JIRA-SRV-789 (microburst tail investigation), JIRA-SRV-804 (kv-cache background write request)

Closure:
This run indicates slice-based isolation is a promising lever to reduce extreme tail latency for interactive workloads. The most pragmatic path forward is an opt-in slice-cap-4 policy with accompanying engineering to remove lock contention and offload cache writes. The team should prioritize follow-up experiments listed above to validate at scale before broad rollout.

-- Maya
summary: Working notes from an experimental campaign testing slice-level isolation in the continuous batching scheduler. Results: slice isolation reduces p99.9 significantly (best p99.9 ~260ms with preemption) but adds small median regression and scheduler overhead. Next steps: lock-free queue, background KV cache writer, beta opt-in rollout behind feature flag.
